entries.052bbd8fe95238491be89794c26df739cdc788c9: <div sID="gen30486" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Rom.3" sID="Rom.3"/> <div eID="gen30486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30487" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30488" type="x-p"/> The apostle, in this chapter, carries on his discourse concerning justification. He had already proved the guilt both of Gentiles and Jews. Now in this chapter, I. He answers some objections that might be made against what he had said about the Jews, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.1-Rom.3.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. He asserts the guilt and corruption of mankind in common, both Jews and Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.9-Rom.3.18">ver. 9-18</reference>. III. He argues thence that justification must needs be by faith, and not by the law, which he gives several reasons for (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.19-Rom.3.31">ver. 19 to the end</reference>). The many digressions in his writings render his discourse sometimes a little difficult, but his scope is evident.
entries.8c92389b2efb62613f789cc28ed9dd41e6250f06: <div eID="gen30488" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30487" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Advantages of the Jews; Objections Answered; The Depravity of Jews and Gentiles. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 58.)</title> <div sID="gen30489" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit <hi type="italic">is there</hi> of circumcision? <hi type="super">2</hi> Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God. 3 For what if some did not believe? shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? <hi type="super">4</hi> God forbid: yea, let God be true, but every man a liar; as it is written, That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and mightest overcome when thou art judged. <hi type="super">5</hi> But if our unrighteousness commend the righteousness of God, what shall we say? <hi type="italic">Is</hi> God unrighteous who taketh vengeance? (I speak as a man) <hi type="super">6</hi> God forbid: for then how shall God judge the world? <hi type="super">7</hi> For if the truth of God hath more abounded through my lie unto his glory; why yet am I also judged as a sinner? <hi type="super">8</hi> And not <hi type="italic">rather,</hi> (as we be slanderously reported, and as some affirm that we say,) Let us do evil, that good may come? whose damnation is just. <hi type="super">9</hi> What then? are we better <hi type="italic">than they?</hi> No, in no wise: for we have before proved both Jews and Gentiles, that they are all under sin; 10 As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one: 11 There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. <hi type="super">12</hi> They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one. <hi type="super">13</hi> Their throat <hi type="italic">is</hi> an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps <hi type="italic">is</hi> under their lips: <hi type="super">14</hi> Whose mouth <hi type="italic">is</hi> full of cursing and bitterness: <hi type="super">15</hi> Their feet <hi type="italic">are</hi> swift to shed blood: <hi type="super">16</hi> Destruction and misery <hi type="italic">are</hi> in their ways: <hi type="super">17</hi> And the way of peace have they not known: <hi type="super">18</hi> There is no fear of God before their eyes. <div eID="gen30489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30490" type="x-p"/> I. Here the apostle answers several objections, which might be made, to clear his way. No truth so plain and evident but wicked wits and corrupt carnal hearts will have something to say against it; but divine truths must be cleared from cavil. <div eID="gen30490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30491" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Object.</hi> 1. If Jew and Gentile stand so much upon the same level before God, <hi type="italic">what advantage then hath the Jew?</hi> Hath not God often spoken with a great deal of respect for the Jews, as a non-such people (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">Deut. xxxiii. 29</reference>), a holy nation, a peculiar treasure, the seed of Abraham his friend: Did not he institute circumcision as a badge of their church-membership, and a seal of their covenant-relation to God? Now does not this levelling doctrine deny them all such prerogatives, and reflect dishonour upon the ordinance of circumcision, as a fruitless insignificant thing. <div eID="gen30491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30492" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Answer.</hi> The Jews are, notwithstanding this, a people greatly privileged and honoured, have great means and helps, though these be not infallibly saving (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Much every way.</hi> The door is open to the Gentiles as well as the Jews, but the Jews have a fairer way up to this door, by reason of their church-privileges, which are not to be undervalued, though many that have them perish eternally for not improving them. He reckons up many of the Jews' privileges <reference osisRef="Rom.9.4-Rom.9.5">Rom. ix. 4, 5</reference>; here he mentions but one (which is indeed <hi type="italic">instar omnium</hi>—<hi type="italic">equivalent to all</hi>), <hi type="italic">that unto them were committed the oracles of God,</hi> that is, the scriptures of the Old Testament, especially the law of Moses, which is called <hi type="italic">the lively oracles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.38">Acts vii. 38</reference>), and those types, promises, and prophecies, which relate to Christ and the gospel. The scriptures are the oracles of God: they are a divine revelation, they come from heaven, are of infallible truth, and of eternal consequence as oracles. The Septuagint call the Urim and Thummim the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">logia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the oracles.</hi> The scripture is our breast-plate of judgment. We must have recourse to the law and to the testimony, as to an oracle. The gospel is called the oracles of God, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.12">Heb. v. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">1 Pet. iv. 11</reference>. Now these oracles were committed to the Jews; the Old Testament was written in their language; Moses and the prophets were of their nation, lived among them, preached and wrote primarily to and for the Jews. They were committed to them as trustees for succeeding ages and churches. The Old Testament was deposited in their hands, to be carefully preserved pure and uncorrupt, and so transmitted down to posterity. The Jews were the Christians' library-keepers, were entrusted with that sacred treasure for their own use and benefit in the first place, and then for the advantage of the world; and, in preserving the letter of the scripture, they were very faithful to their trust, did not lose one iota or tittle, in which we are to acknowledge God's gracious care and providence. The Jews had the means of salvation, but they had not the monopoly of salvation. Now this he mentions with a <hi type="italic">chiefly,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">proton men gar</hi></hi>—this was their prime and principal privilege. The enjoyment of God's word and ordinances is the chief happiness of a people, is to be put in the <hi type="italic">imprimis</hi> of their advantages, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.8">Deut. iv. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.3">xxxiii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.147.20">Ps. cxlvii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen30492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30493" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Object.</hi> 2. Against what he had said of the advantages the Jews had in the lively oracles, some might object the unbelief of many of them. To what purpose were the oracles of God committed to them, when so many of them, notwithstanding these oracles, continued strangers to Christ, and enemies to his gospel? <hi type="italic">Some did not believe,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.3">v. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen30493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30494" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Answer.</hi> It is very true that some, nay most of the present Jews, do not believe in Christ; <hi type="italic">but shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect?</hi> The apostle startles at such a thought: <hi type="italic">God forbid!</hi> The infidelity and obstinacy of the Jews could not invalidate and overthrow those prophecies of the Messiah which were contained in the oracles committed to them. Christ will be glorious, <hi type="italic">though Israel be not gathered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">Isa. xlix. 5</reference>. God's words shall be accomplished, his purposes performed, and all his ends answered, though there be a generation that by their unbelief go about to make God a liar. <hi type="italic">Let God be true but every man a liar;</hi> let us abide by this principle, that God is true to every word which he has spoken, and will let none of his oracles fall to the ground, though thereby we give the lie to man; better question and overthrow the credit of all the men in the world than doubt of the faithfulness of God. What David said in his haste (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.11">Ps. cxvi. 11</reference>), that all men are liars, Paul here asserts deliberately. Lying is a limb of that old man which we every one of us come into the world clothed with. All men are fickle, and mutable, and given to change, <hi type="italic">vanity and a lie</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.62.9">Ps. lxii. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">altogether vanity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.39.5">Ps. xxxix. 5</reference>. All men are liars, compared with God. It is very comfortable, when we find every man a liar (no faith in man), that God is faithful. When <hi type="italic">they speak vanity every one with his neighbour,</hi> it is very comfortable to think <hi type="italic">that the words of the Lord are pure words,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.12.2">Ps. xii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.12.6">6</reference>. For the further proof of this he quotes <reference osisRef="Ps.51.4">Ps. li. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">That thou mightest be justified,</hi> the design of which is to show, 1. That God does and will preserve his own honour in the world, notwithstanding the sins of men. 2. That it is our duty, in all our conclusions concerning ourselves and others, to justify God and to assert and maintain his justice, truth, and goodness, however it goes. David lays a load upon himself in his confession, that he might justify God, and acquit him from any injustice. So here, Let the credit or reputation of man shift for itself, the matter is not great whether it sink or swim; let us hold fast this conclusion, how specious soever the premises may be to the contrary, that <hi type="italic">the Lord is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works.</hi> Thus is God justified in his sayings, and cleared when he judges (as it is <reference osisRef="Ps.51.4">Ps. li. 4</reference>), or when <hi type="italic">he is judged,</hi> as it is here rendered. When men presume to quarrel with God and his proceedings, we may be sure the sentence will go on God's side. <div eID="gen30494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30495" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Object.</hi> 3. Carnal hearts might hence take occasion to encourage themselves in sin. He had said that the universal guilt and corruption of mankind gave occasion to the manifestation of God's righteousness in Jesus Christ. Now it may be suggested, If all our sin be so far from overthrowing God's honour that it commends it, and his ends are secured, so that there is no harm done, is it not unjust for God to punish our sin and unbelief so severely? If the unrighteousness of the Jews gave occasion to the calling in of the Gentiles, and so to God's greater glory, why are the Jews so much censured? <hi type="italic">If our unrighteousness commend the righteousness of God, what shall we say?</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.5">v. 5</reference>. What inference may be drawn from this? <hi type="italic">Is God unrighteous,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">me adikos ho Theos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Is not God unrighteous</hi> (so it may be read, more in the form of an objection), <hi type="italic">who taketh vengeance?</hi> Unbelieving hearts will gladly take any occasion to quarrel with equity of God's proceedings, and to condemn him that is most just, <reference osisRef="Job.34.17">Job xxxiv. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">I speak as a man,</hi> that is, I object this as those of carnal hearts; it is suggested like a man, a vain, foolish, proud creature. <div eID="gen30495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30496" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Answer. God forbid;</hi> far be it from us to imagine such a thing. Suggestions that reflect dishonour upon God and his justice and holiness are rather to be startled at than parleyed with. Get thee behind me, Satan; never entertain such a thought. <hi type="italic">For then how shall God judge the world?</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.6">v. 6</reference>. The argument is much the same with that of Abraham (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.25">Gen. xviii. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?</hi> No doubt, he shall. If he were not infinitely just and righteous, he would be unfit to be the judge of all the earth. <hi type="italic">Shall even he that hateth right govern?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.34.17">Job xxxiv. 17</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.3.18-Rom.3.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. The sin has never the less of malignity and demerit in it though God bring glory to himself out of it. It is only accidentally that sin commends God's righteousness. No thanks to the sinner for that, who intends no such thing. The consideration of God's judging the world should for ever silence all our doubtings of, and reflections upon, his justice and equity. It is not for us to arraign the proceedings of such an absolute Sovereign. The sentence of the supreme court, whence lies no appeal, is not to be called in question. <div eID="gen30496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30497" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Object.</hi> 4. The former objection is repeated and prosecuted (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.7-Rom.3.8">v. 7, 8</reference>), for proud hearts will hardly be beaten out of their refuge of lies, but will hold fast the deceit. But his setting off the objection in its own colours is sufficient to answer it: <hi type="italic">If the truth of God has more abounded through my lie.</hi> He supposes the sophisters to follow their objection thus: "If my lie, that is, my sin" (for there is something of a lie in every sin, especially in the sins of professors) "have occasioned the glorifying of God's truth and faithfulness, why <hi type="italic">should I be judged</hi> and condemned <hi type="italic">as a sinner, and not rather</hi> thence take encouragement to go on in my sin, that grace may abound?" an inference which at first sight appears too black to be argued, and fit to be cast out with abhorrence. Daring sinners take occasion to boast in mischief, because the <hi type="italic">goodness of God endures continually,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.52.1">Ps. lii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Let us do evil that good may come</hi> is oftener in the heart than in the mouth of sinners, so justifying themselves in their wicked ways. Mentioning this wicked thought, he observes, in a parenthesis, that there were those who charged such doctrines as this upon Paul and his fellow-ministers: Some affirm that we say so. It is no new thing for the best of God's people and ministers to be charged with holding and teaching such things as they do most detest and abhor; and it is not to be thought strange, when our Master himself was said to be in league with Beelzebub. Many have been reproached as if they had said that the contrary of which they maintain: it is an old artifice of Satan thus to cast dirt upon Christ's ministers, <hi type="italic">Fortiter calumniari, aliquid adhærebit—Lay slander thickly on, for some will be sure to stick.</hi> The best men and the best truths are subject to slander. Bishop Sanderson makes a further remark upon this, <hi type="italic">as we are slanderously reported</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">blasphemoumetha.</hi></hi> Blasphemy in scripture usually signifies the highest degree of slander, speaking ill of God. The slander of a minister and his regular doctrine is a more than ordinary slander, it is a kind of blasphemy, not for his person's sake, but for his calling's sake and his work's sake, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.13">1 Thess. v. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen30497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30498" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Answer.</hi> He says no more by way of confutation but that, whatever they themselves may argue, the damnation of those is just. Some understand it of the slanderers; God will justly condemn those who unjustly condemn his truth. Or, rather, it is to be applied to those who embolden themselves in sin under a pretence of God's getting glory to himself out of it. Those who deliberately do evil that good may come of it will be so far from escaping, under the shelter of that excuse, that it will rather justify their damnation, and render them the more inexcusable; for sinning upon such a surmise, and in such a confidence, argues a great deal both of the wit and of the will in the sin—a wicked will deliberately to choose the evil, and a wicked wit to palliate it with the pretence of good arising from it. Therefore their damnation is just; and, whatever excuses of this kind they may now please themselves with, they will none of them stand good in the great day, but God will be justified in his proceedings, and all flesh, even the proud flesh that now lifts up itself against him, shall be silent before him. Some think Paul herein refers to the approaching ruin of the Jewish church and nation, which their obstinacy and self-justification in their unbelief hastened upon them apace. <div eID="gen30498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30499" type="x-p"/> II. Paul, having removed these objections, next revives his assertion of the general guilt and corruption of mankind in common, both of Jews and Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.9-Rom.3.18">v. 9-18</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Are we better than they,</hi> we Jews, to whom were committed the oracles of God? Does this recommend us to God, or will this justify us? No, by no means." Or, "Are we Christians (Jews and Gentiles) so much better antecedently than the unbelieving part as to have merited God's grace? Alas! no: before free grace made the difference, those of us that had been Jews and those that had been Gentiles were all alike corrupted." They <hi type="italic">are all under sin.</hi> Under the guilt of sin: under it as under a sentence;—under it as under a bond, by which they are bound over to eternal ruin and damnation;—under it as under a burden (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.4">Ps. xxxviii. 4</reference>) that will sink them to the lowest hell: we are guilty before God, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.19">v. 19</reference>. Under the government and dominion of sin: under it as under a tyrant and cruel task-master, enslaved to it;—under it as under a yoke;—under the power of it, sold to work wickedness. And this he had proved, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">proetiasametha.</hi></hi> It is a law term: <hi type="italic">We have charged them with it,</hi> and have made good our charge; we have proved the indictment, we have convicted them by the notorious evidence of the fact. This charge and conviction he here further illustrates by several scriptures out of the Old Testament, which describe the corrupt depraved state of all men, till grave restrain or change them; so that herein as in a glass we may all of us behold our natural face. The <reference osisRef="Rom.3.10-Rom.3.12">10th, 11th</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.3">and 12th verses</reference> are taken from <reference osisRef="Rom.3.10-Rom.3.12 Ps.14.1-Ps.14.3">Ps. xiv. 1-3</reference>, which are repeated as containing a very weighty truth, <reference osisRef="Ps.53.1-Ps.53.3 Ps.14.1-Ps.14.3">Ps. liii. 1-3</reference>. The rest that follows here is found in the Septuagint translation of the <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">14th Psalm</reference>, which some think the apostle chooses to follow as better known; but I rather think that Paul took these passages from other places of scripture here referred to, but in later copies of the LXX. they were all added in <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Ps. xiv.</reference> from this discourse of Paul. It is observable that, to prove the general corruption of nature, he quotes some scriptures which speak of the particular corruptions of particular persons, as of Doeg (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.3">Ps. cxl. 3</reference>), of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.7-Isa.59.8">Isa. lix. 7, 8</reference>), which shows that the same sins that are committed by one are in the nature of all. The times of David and Isaiah were some of the better times, and yet to their days he refers. What is said <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7">Ps. xiv.</reference> is expressly spoken of <hi type="italic">all the children of men,</hi> and that upon a particular view and inspection made by God himself. The <hi type="italic">Lord looked down,</hi> as upon the old world, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.5">Gen. vi. 5</reference>. And this judgment of God was according to truth. He who, when he himself had made all, looked upon every thing that he had made, and behold all was very good, now that man had marred all, looked, and behold all was very bad. Let us take a view of the particulars. Observe, <div eID="gen30499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30500" type="x-p"/> 1. That which is habitual, which is two-fold:— <div eID="gen30500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30501" type="x-p"/> (1.) An habitual defect of every thing that is good. [1.] <hi type="italic">There is none righteous,</hi> none that has an honest good principle of virtue, or is governed by such a principle, none that retains any thing of that image of God, consisting in righteousness, wherein man was created; <hi type="italic">no, not one;</hi> implying that, if there had been but one, God would have found him out. When all the world was corrupt, God had his eye upon one righteous Noah. Even those who through grace are justified and sanctified were none of them righteous by nature. No righteousness is born with us. The man after God's own heart owns himself conceived in sin. [2.] <hi type="italic">There is none that understandeth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.11">v. 11</reference>. The fault lies in the corruption of the understanding; that is blinded, depraved, perverted. Religion and righteousness have so much reason on their side that if people had but any understanding they would be better and do better. But they do not understand. Sinners are fools. [3.] <hi type="italic">None that seeketh after God,</hi> that is, none that has any regard to God, any desire after him. Those may justly be reckoned to have no understanding that do not seek after God. The carnal mind is so far from seeking after God that really it is enmity against him. [4.] <hi type="italic">They are together become unprofitable,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.12">v. 12</reference>. Those that have forsaken God soon grow good for nothing, useless burdens of the earth. Those that are in a state of sin are the most unprofitable creatures under the sun; for it follows, [5.] <hi type="italic">There is none that doeth good;</hi> no, not a just man upon the earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.23">Eccl. vii. 23</reference>. Even in those actions of sinners that have some goodness in them there is a fundamental error in the principle and end; so that it may be said, There is none that doeth good. <hi type="italic">Malum oritur ex quolibet defectu—Every defect is the source of evil.</hi> <div eID="gen30501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30502" type="x-p"/> (2.) An habitual defection to every thing that is evil: <hi type="italic">They are all gone out of the way.</hi> No wonder that those miss the right way who do not seek after God, the highest end. God made man in the way, set him in right, but he hath forsaken it. The corruption of mankind is an apostasy. <div eID="gen30502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30503" type="x-p"/> 2. That which is actual. And what good can be expected from such a degenerate race? He instances, <div eID="gen30503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30504" type="x-p"/> (1.) In their words (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.13-Rom.3.14">v. 13, 14</reference>), in three things particularly:—[1.] Cruelty: <hi type="italic">Their throat is an open sepulchre,</hi> ready to swallow up the poor and innocent, waiting an opportunity to do mischief, like the old serpent seeking to devour, whose name is Abaddon and Apollyon, the destroyer. And when they do not openly avow this cruelty, and vent it publicly, yet they are underhand intending mischief: the <hi type="italic">poison of asps is under their lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.8">Jam. iii. 8</reference>), the most venomous and incurable poison, with which they blast the good name of their neighbour by reproaches, and aim at his life by false witness. These passages are borrowed from <reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Ps. v. 9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.140.3">cxl. 3</reference>. [2.] Cheating: <hi type="italic">With their tongues they have used deceit.</hi> Herein they show themselves the devil's children, for he is a liar, and the father of lies. They <hi type="italic">have used</hi> it: it intimates that they make a trade of lying; it is their constant practice, especially belying the ways and people of God. [3.] Cursing: reflecting upon God, and blaspheming his holy name; wishing evil to their brethren: <hi type="italic">Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.</hi> This is mentioned as one of the great sins of the tongue, <reference osisRef="Jas.3.9">Jam. iii. 9</reference>. But those that thus love cursing shall have enough of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.109.17-Ps.109.19">Ps. cix. 17-19</reference>. How many, who are called Christians, do by these sin evince that they are still under the reign and dominion of sin, still in the condition that they were born in. <div eID="gen30504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30505" type="x-p"/> (2.) In their ways (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.15-Rom.3.17">v. 15-17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Their feet are swift to shed blood;</hi> that is, they are very industrious to compass any cruel design, ready to lay hold of all such opportunities. Wherever they go, <hi type="italic">destruction and misery</hi> go along with them; these are their companions—destruction and misery to the people of God, to the country and neighbourhood where they live, to the land and nation, and to themselves at last. Besides the destruction and misery that are at the end of their ways (death is the end of these things), destruction and misery are in their ways; their sin is its own punishment: a man needs no more to make him miserable than to be a slave to his sins.—<hi type="italic">And the way of peace have they not known;</hi> that is, they know not how to preserve peace with others, nor how to obtain peace for themselves. They may talk of peace, such a peace as is in the devil's palace, while he keeps it, but they are strangers to all true peace; they know not the things that belong to their peace. These are quoted from <reference osisRef="Prov.1.16">Prov. i. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.7-Isa.59.8">Isa. lix. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen30505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30506" type="x-p"/> (3.) The root of all this we have: <hi type="italic">There is no fear of God before their eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.18">v. 18</reference>. The fear of God is here put for all practical religion, which consists in an awful and serious regard to the word and will of God as our rule, to the honour and glory of God as our end. Wicked people have not this before their eyes; that is, they do not steer by it; they are governed by other rules, aim at other ends. This is quoted from <reference osisRef="Ps.36.1">Ps. xxxvi. 1</reference>. Where no fear of God is, no good is to be expected. The fear of God should lay a restraint upon our spirits, and keep them right, <reference osisRef="Neh.5.15">Neh. v. 15</reference>. When once fear is cast off, prayer is restrained (<reference osisRef="Job.15.4">Job xv. 4</reference>), and then all goes to wreck and ruin quickly. So that we have here a short account of the general depravity and corruption of mankind; and may say, O Adam! what hast thou done? God made man upright, but thus he hath sought out many inventions.
entries.e0499fab90139db08970e272c5bcd1a45af70c35: <div eID="gen30506" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Justification by Faith; Christ a Propitiation. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 58.)</title> <div sID="gen30507" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God. <hi type="super">20</hi> Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law <hi type="italic">is</hi> the knowledge of sin. <hi type="super">21</hi> But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; <hi type="super">22</hi> Even the righteousness of God <hi type="italic">which is</hi> by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference: <hi type="super">23</hi> For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; <hi type="super">24</hi> Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: <hi type="super">25</hi> Whom God hath set forth <hi type="italic">to be</hi> a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God; <hi type="super">26</hi> To declare, <hi type="italic">I say,</hi> at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. <hi type="super">27</hi> Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> boasting then? It is excluded. By what law? of works? Nay: but by the law of faith. <hi type="super">28</hi> Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. 29 <hi type="italic">Is he</hi> the God of the Jews only? <hi type="italic">is he</hi> not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also: <hi type="super">30</hi> Seeing <hi type="italic">it is</hi> one God, which shall justify the circumcision by faith, and uncircumcision through faith. <hi type="super">31</hi> Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law. <div eID="gen30507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30508" type="x-p"/> From all this Paul infers that it is in vain to look for justification by the works of the law, and that it is to be had only by faith, which is the point he has been all along proving, from <reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">ch. i. 17</reference>, and which he lays down (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.28">v. 28</reference>) as the summary of his discourse, with a <hi type="italic">quod erat demonstrandum—which was to be demonstrated. We conclude that a man is justified by faith, without the deeds of the law;</hi> not by the deeds of the first law of pure innocence, which left no room for repentance, nor the deeds of the law of nature, how highly soever improved, nor the deeds of the ceremonial law (the blood of bulls and goats could not take away sin), nor the deeds of the moral law, which are certainly included, for he speaks of that law by which is the knowledge of sin and those works which might be matter of boasting. Man, in his depraved state, under the power of such corruption, could never, by any works of his own, gain acceptance with God; but it must be resolved purely into the free grace of God, given through Jesus Christ to all true believers that receive it as a free gift. If we had never sinned, our obedience to the law would have been our righteousness: "Do this, and live." But having sinned, and being corrupted, nothing that we can do will atone for our former guilt. It was by their obedience to the moral law that the Pharisees looked for justification, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.11">Luke xviii. 11</reference>. Now there are two things from which the apostle here argues: the guiltiness of man, to prove that we cannot be justified by the works of the law, and the glory of God, to prove that we must be justified by faith. <div eID="gen30508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30509" type="x-p"/> I. He argues from man's guiltiness, to show the folly of expecting justification by the works of the law. The argument is very plain: we can never be justified and saved by the law that we have broken. A convicted traitor can never come off by pleading the statute of 25 <hi type="italic">Edward</hi> III., for that law discovers his crime and condemns him: indeed, if he had never broken it, he might have been justified by it; but now it is past that he has broken it, and there is no way of coming off but by pleading the act of indemnity, upon which he has surrendered and submitted himself, and humbly and penitently claiming the benefit of it and casting himself upon it. Now concerning the guiltiness of man, <div eID="gen30509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30510" type="x-p"/> 1. He fastens it particularly upon the Jews; for they were the men that made their boast of the law, and set up for justification by it. He had quoted several scriptures out of the Old Testament to show this corruption: Now, says he (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.19">v. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">this that the law says, it says to those who are under the law;</hi> this conviction belongs to the Jews as well as others, for it is written in their law. The Jews boasted of their being under the law, and placed a great deal of confidence in it: "But," says he, "the law convicts and condemns you—you see it does." That <hi type="italic">every mouth may be stopped</hi>—that all boasting may be silenced. See the method that God takes both in justifying and condemning: he stops every mouth; those that are justified have their mouths stopped by a humble conviction; those that are condemned have their mouths stopped too, for they shall at last be convinced (<reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>), and sent speechless to hell, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.12">Matt. xxii. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">All iniquity shall stop her mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.42">Ps. cvii. 42</reference>. <div eID="gen30510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30511" type="x-p"/> 2. He extends it in general to all the world: <hi type="italic">That all the world may become guilty before God.</hi> If the world lieth in wickedness (<reference osisRef="1John.5.19">1 John v. 19</reference>), to be sure it is guilty.—<hi type="italic">May become guilty;</hi> that is, may be proved guilty, liable to punishment, all by nature <hi type="italic">children of wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.3">Eph. ii. 3</reference>. They must all plead guilty; those that stand most upon their own justification will certainly be cast. Guilty before God is a dreadful word, before an all-seeing God, that is not, nor can be, deceived in his judgment—before a just and righteous judge, who will by no means clear the guilty. All are guilty, and therefore all have need of a righteousness wherein to appear before God. <hi type="italic">For all have sinned</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.23">v. 23</reference>); all are sinners by nature, by practice, and <hi type="italic">have come short of the glory of God</hi>—have failed of that which is the chief end of man. <hi type="italic">Come short,</hi> as the archer comes short of the mark, as the runner comes short of the prize; so come short, as not only not to win, but to be great losers. <hi type="italic">Come short of the glory of God.</hi> (1.) Come short of glorifying God. See <reference osisRef="Rom.1.21">ch. i. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">They glorified him not as God.</hi> Man was placed at the head of the visible creation, actively to glorify that great Creator whom the inferior creatures could glorify only objectively; but man by sin comes short of this, and, instead of glorifying God, dishonours him. It is a very melancholy consideration, to look upon the children of men, who were made to glorify God, and to think how few there are that do it. (2.) Come short of glorying <hi type="italic">before God.</hi> There is no boasting of innocency: if we go about to glory before God, to boast of any thing we are, or have, or do, this will be an everlasting estoppel—that we have all sinned, and this will silence us. We may glory before men, who are short-sighted, and cannot search our hearts,—who are corrupt, as we are, and well enough pleased with sin; but there is no glorying before God, who cannot endure to look upon iniquity. (3.) Come short of being glorified by God. Come short of justification, or acceptance with God, which is glory begun—come short of the holiness or sanctification which is the glorious image of God upon man, and have overthrown all hopes and expectations of being glorified with God in heaven by any righteousness of their own. It is impossible now to get to heaven in the way of spotless innocency. That passage is blocked up. There is a cherub and a flaming sword set to keep that way to the tree of life. <div eID="gen30511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30512" type="x-p"/> 3. Further to drive us off from expecting justification by the law, he ascribes this conviction to the law (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">For by the law is the knowledge of sin.</hi> That law which convicts and condemns us can never justify us. The law is the straight rule, that <hi type="italic">rectum</hi> which is <hi type="italic">index sui et obliqui—that which points out the right and the wrong;</hi> it is the proper use and intendment of the law to open our wound, and therefore not likely to be the remedy. That which is searching is not sanative. Those that would know sin must get the knowledge of the law in its strictness, extent, and spiritual nature. If we compare our own hearts and lives with the rule, we shall discover wherein we have turned aside. Paul makes this use of the law, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.9">ch. vii. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">Therefore by the deeds of the law shall no flesh be justified in his sight.</hi> Observe, (1.) <hi type="italic">No flesh shall be justified,</hi> no man, no corrupted man (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.3">Gen. vi. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">for that he also is flesh,</hi> sinful and depraved; therefore not justified, because we are flesh. The corruption that remains in our nature will for ever obstruct any justification by our own works, which, coming from flesh, must needs taste of the cask, <reference osisRef="Job.14.4">Job xiv. 4</reference>. (2.) Not justified in his sight. He does not deny that justification which was by the deeds of the law in the sight of the church: they were, in their church-estate, as embodied in a polity, a holy people, a nation of priests; but as the conscience stands in relation to God, <hi type="italic">in his sight,</hi> we cannot be justified by the deeds of the law. The apostle refers to <reference osisRef="Ps.143.2">Ps. cxliii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen30512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30513" type="x-p"/> II. He argues from God's glory to prove that justification must be expected only by faith in Christ's righteousness. There is no justification by the works of the law. Must guilty man then remain eternally under wrath? Is there no hope? Is the wound become incurable because of transgression? No, blessed be God, it is not (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.21-Rom.3.22">v. 21, 22</reference>); there is another way laid open for us, <hi type="italic">the righteousness of God without the law is manifested</hi> now under the gospel. Justification may be obtained without the keeping of Moses's law: and this is called <hi type="italic">the righteousness of God,</hi> righteousness of his ordaining, and providing, and accepting,—righteousness which he confers upon us; as the Christian armour is called <hi type="italic">the armour of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.11">Eph. vi. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen30513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30514" type="x-p"/> 1. Now concerning this righteousness of God observe, (1.) That it is manifested. The gospel-way of justification is a high-way, a plain way, it is laid open for us: the brazen serpent is lifted up upon the pole; we are not left to grope our way in the dark, but it is manifested to us. (2.) It is <hi type="italic">without the law.</hi> Here he obviates the method of the judaizing Christians, who would needs join Christ and Moses together—owning Christ for the Messiah, and yet too fondly retaining the law, keeping up the ceremonies of it, and imposing it upon the Gentile converts: no, says he, it is without the law. The righteousness that Christ hath brought in is a complete righteousness. (3.) Yet <hi type="italic">it is witnessed by the law and the prophets;</hi> that is, there were types, and prophecies, and promises, in the Old Testament, that pointed at this. The law is so far from justifying us that it directs us to another way of justification, points at Christ as our righteousness, to whom bear all the prophets witness. See <reference osisRef="Acts.10.43">Acts x. 43</reference>. This might recommend it to the Jews, who were so fond of the law and the prophets. (4.) It is by the <hi type="italic">faith of Jesus Christ,</hi> that faith which hath Jesus Christ for its object—an <hi type="italic">anointed Saviour,</hi> so Jesus Christ signifies. Justifying faith respects Christ as a Saviour in all his three anointed offices, as prophet, priest, and king—trusting in him, accepting of him, and adhering to him, in all these. It is by this that we become interested in that righteousness which God has ordained, and which Christ has brought in. (5.) It is <hi type="italic">to all, and upon all, those that believe.</hi> In this expression he inculcates that which he had been often harping upon, that Jews and Gentiles, if they believe, stand upon the same level, and are alike welcome to God through Christ; <hi type="italic">for there is no difference.</hi> Or, it is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eis pantas</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to all,</hi> offered to all in general; the gospel excludes none that do not exclude themselves; but it is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epi pantas tous pisteuontas,</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">upon all that believe,</hi> not only tendered to them, but put upon them as a crown, as a robe; they are, upon their believing, interested in it, and entitled to all the benefits and privileges of it. <div eID="gen30514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30515" type="x-p"/> 2. But now how is this for God's glory? <div eID="gen30515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30516" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is for the glory of his grace (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Justified freely by his grace</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dorean te autou chariti.</hi></hi> It is <hi type="italic">by his grace,</hi> not by the grace wrought in us as the papists say, confounding justification and sanctification, but by the gracious favour of God to us, without any merit in us so much as foreseen. And, to make it the more emphatic, he says it is <hi type="italic">freely by his grace,</hi> to show that it must be understood of grace in the most proper and genuine sense. It is said that <hi type="italic">Joseph found grace</hi> in the sight of his master (<reference osisRef="Gen.39.4">Gen. xxxix. 4</reference>), but there was a reason; he saw that what he did prospered. There was something in Joseph to invite that grace; but the grace of God communicated to us comes <hi type="italic">freely, freely;</hi> it is free grace, mere mercy; nothing in us to deserve such favours: no, it is all <hi type="italic">through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ.</hi> It comes freely to us, but Christ bought it, and paid dearly for it, which yet is so ordered as not to derogate from the honour of free grace. Christ's purchase is no bar to the freeness of God's grace; for grace provided and accepted this vicarious satisfaction. <div eID="gen30516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30517" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is for the glory of his justice and righteousness (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.25-Rom.3.26">v. 25, 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation,</hi> &c. Note, [1.] Jesus Christ is the great propitiation, or propitiatory sacrifice, typified by the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hilasterion,</hi></hi> or <hi type="italic">mercy-seat,</hi> under the law. He is our throne of grace, in and through whom atonement is made for sin, and our persons and performances are accepted of God, <reference osisRef="1John.2.2">1 John ii. 2</reference>. He is all in all in our reconciliation, not only the maker, but the matter of it—our priest, our sacrifice, our altar, our all. God was in Christ as in his mercy-seat, reconciling the world unto himself. [2.] <hi type="italic">God hath set him forth</hi> to be so. God, the party offended, makes the first overtures towards a reconciliation, appoints the days-man; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">proetheto</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">fore-ordained</hi> him to this, in the counsels of his love from eternity, appointed, anointed him to it, qualified him for it, and has exhibited him to a guilty world as their propitiation. See <reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Matt. iii. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">and xvii. 5</reference>. [3.] That <hi type="italic">by faith in his blood</hi> we become interested in this propitiation. Christ is the propitiation; there is the healing plaster provided. Faith is the applying of this plaster to the wounded soul. And this faith in the business of justification hath a special regard to <hi type="italic">the blood of Christ,</hi> as that which made the atonement; for such was the divine appointment that without blood there should be no remission, and no blood but his would do it effectually. Here may be an allusion to the sprinkling of the blood of the sacrifices under the law, as <reference osisRef="Exod.24.8">Exod. xxiv. 8</reference>. Faith is the bunch of hyssop, and the blood of Christ is the blood of sprinkling. [4.] That all who by faith are interested in this propitiation have <hi type="italic">the remission of their sins that are past.</hi> It was for this that Christ was set forth to be a propitiation, in order to remission, to which the reprieves of his patience and forbearance were a very encouraging preface. <hi type="italic">Through the forbearance of God.</hi> Divine patience has kept us out of hell, that we might have space to repent, and get to heaven. Some refer the <hi type="italic">sins that are past</hi> to the sins of the Old-Testament saints, which were pardoned for the sake of the atonement which Christ in the fulness of time was to make, which looked backward as well as forward. <hi type="italic">Past through the forbearance of God.</hi> It is owing to the divine forbearance that we were not taken in the very act of sin. Several Greek copies make <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en te anoche tou Theou</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">through the forbearance of God,</hi> to begin <reference osisRef="Rom.3.26">v. 26</reference>, and they denote two precious fruits of Christ's merit and God's grace:—Remission: <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dia ten paresin</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">for the remission;</hi> and reprieves: the <hi type="italic">forbearance</hi> of God. It is owing to the master's goodness and the dresser's mediation that barren trees are let alone in the vineyard; and in both God's righteousness is declared, in that without a mediator and a propitiation he would not only not pardon, but not so much as forbear, not spare a moment; it is owning to Christ that there is ever a sinner on this side hell. [5.] That God does in all this <hi type="italic">declare his righteousness.</hi> This he insists upon with a great deal of emphasis: <hi type="italic">To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness.</hi> It is repeated, as that which has in it something surprising. He declares his righteousness, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In the propitiation itself. Never was there such a demonstration of the justice and holiness of God as there was in the death of Christ. It appears that he hates sin, when nothing less than the blood of Christ would satisfy for it. Finding sin, though but imputed, upon his own Son, he did not spare him, because he had made himself sin for us, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2 Cor. v. 21</reference>. The iniquities of us all being laid upon him, though he was the Son of his love, yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa. liii. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In the pardon upon that propitiation; so it follows, by way of explication: <hi type="italic">That he might be just, and the justifier of him that believeth.</hi> Mercy and truth are so met together, righteousness and peace have so kissed each other, that it is now become not only an act of grace and mercy, but an act of righteousness, in God, to pardon the sins of penitent believers, having accepted the satisfaction that Christ by dying made to his justice for them. It would not comport with his justice to demand the debt of the principal when the surety has paid it and he has accepted that payment in full satisfaction. See <reference osisRef="1John.1.9">1 John i. 9</reference>. He is just, that is, faithful to his word. <div eID="gen30517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30518" type="x-p"/> (3.) It is for God's glory; for boasting is thus excluded, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.27">v. 27</reference>. God will have the great work of the justification and salvation of sinners carried on from first to last in such a way as to exclude boasting, that no flesh may glory in his presence, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.29-1Cor.1.31">1 Cor. i. 29-31</reference>. Now, if justification were by the works of the law, boasting would not be excluded. How should it? If we were saved by our own works, we might put the crown upon our own heads. But the <hi type="italic">law of faith,</hi> that is, the way of justification by faith, doth for ever exclude boasting; for faith is a depending, self-emptying, self-denying grace, and casts every crown before the throne; therefore it is most for God's glory that thus we should be justified. Observe, He speaks of <hi type="italic">the law of faith.</hi> Believers are not left lawless: faith is a law, it is a working grace, wherever it is in truth; and yet, because it acts in a strict and close dependence upon Jesus Christ, it excludes boasting. <div eID="gen30518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30519" type="x-p"/> From all this he draws this conclusion (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">That a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.</hi> <div eID="gen30519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30520" type="x-p"/> III. In the close of the chapter he shows the extent of this privilege of justification by faith, and that it is not the peculiar privilege of the Jews, but pertains to the Gentiles also; for he had said (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.22">v. 22</reference>) that there is no difference: and as to this, 1. He asserts and proves it (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">Is he the God of the Jews only?</hi> He argues from the absurdity of such a supposition. Can it be imagined that a God of infinite love and mercy should limit and confine his favours to that little perverse people of the Jews, leaving all the rest of the children of men in a condition eternally desperate? This would by no means agree with the idea we have of the divine goodness, for his <hi type="italic">tender mercies are over all his works;</hi> therefore it is one God of grace that <hi type="italic">justifies the circumcision by faith, and the uncircumcision through faith,</hi> that is, both in one and the same way. However the Jews, in favour of themselves, will needs fancy a difference, really there is no more difference than between <hi type="italic">by</hi> and <hi type="italic">through,</hi> that is, no difference at all. 2. He obviates an objection (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.31">v. 31</reference>), as if this doctrine did nullify the law, which they knew came from God: "No," says he, "though we do say that the law will not justify us, yet we do not therefore say that it was given in vain, or is of no use to us; no, <hi type="italic">we establish the right use of the law,</hi> and secure its standing, by fixing it on the right basis. The law is still of use to convince us of what is past, and to direct us for the future; though we cannot be saved by it as a covenant, yet we own it, and submit to it, as a rule in the hand of the Mediator, subordinate to the law of grace; and so are so far from overthrowing that we establish the law." Let those consider this who deny the obligation of the moral law on believers.  <chapter eID="Rom.3"/> <div eID="gen30520" type="x-p"/>

What advantage then hath the Jew?--</hi>that is, "If the final judgment will turn solely on the state of the heart, and this may be as good in the Gentile without, as in the Jew within, the sacred enclosure of God's covenant, what better are we Jews for all our advantages?"<div eID="gen31775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31776" type="x-p"/> Answer: <div eID="gen31776" type="x-p"/>

For what if some did not believe?--</hi>It is the unbelief of the great body of the nation which the apostle points at; but as it sufficed for his argument to put the supposition thus gently, he uses this word "some" to soften prejudice.<div eID="gen31779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall their unbelief make the faith of God--</hi>or, "faithfulness of God."<div eID="gen31780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of none effect?--</hi>"nullify," "invalidate" it. <div eID="gen31781" type="x-p"/>

But if, &c.--</hi>Another objection: "It would appear, then, that the more faithless we are, so much the more illustrious will the fidelity of God appear; and in that case, for Him to take vengeance on us for our unfaithfulness would be (to speak as men profanely do) unrighteousness in God."<div eID="gen31786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31787" type="x-p"/> Answer: <div eID="gen31787" type="x-p"/>
entries.9953cc0cb60a0880a47325c7d6284fe419122872: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16390"/><div sID="gen31789" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16390"/><hi type="bold">7-8. For if the truth of God, &c.--</hi>A further illustration of the same sentiment: that is, "Such reasoning amounts to this--which indeed we who preach salvation by free grace are slanderously accused of teaching--that the more evil we do, the more glory will redound to God; a damnable principle." (Thus the apostle, instead of refuting this principle, thinks it enough to hold it up to execration, as one that shocks the moral sense).<div eID="gen31789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31790" type="x-p"/> On this brief section, Note (1) Mark the place here assigned to the Scriptures. In answer to the question, "What advantage hath the Jew?" or, "What profit is there of circumcision?" (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.1">Ro 3:1</reference>) those holding Romish views would undoubtedly have laid the stress upon the priesthood, as the glory of the Jewish economy. But in the apostle's esteem, "the oracles of God" were the jewel of the ancient Church (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.1">Ro 3:1</reference>, 2). (2) God's eternal purposes and man's free agency, as also the doctrine of salvation by grace and the unchanging obligations of God's law, have ever been subjected to the charge of inconsistency by those who will bow to no truth which their own reason cannot fathom. But amidst all the clouds and darkness which in this present state envelop the divine administration and many of the truths of the Bible, such broad and deep principles as are here laid down, and which shine in their own luster, will be found the sheet-anchor of our faith. "Let God be true, and every man a liar" (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.4">Ro 3:4</reference>); and as many advocates of salvation by grace as say, "Let us do evil that good may come," "their damnation is just" (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.8">Ro 3:8</reference>). <div eID="gen31790" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6c24d600d39ec650e5d09d7b102569aa586fbd1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16391"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Rom.3.9-Rom.3.20">Ro 3:9-20</reference>. That the Jew Is Shut Up under Like Condemnation with the Gentile Is Proved by His Own Scripture.</title> <div sID="gen31791" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16391"/><hi type="bold">9. are we better than they?--</hi>"do we excel them?"<div eID="gen31791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">No, in no wise--</hi>Better off the Jews certainly were, for having the oracles of God to teach them better; but as they were no better, that only aggravated their guilt. <div eID="gen31792" type="x-p"/>
entries.249bb0262a8bb45d8b3f95a9673b0d5f8c54a7d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16392"/><div sID="gen31793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16392"/><hi type="bold">10-12. As it is written, &c.--</hi>(Psa 14:1-3; 53:1-3). These statements of the Psalmist were indeed suggested by particular manifestations of human depravity occurring under his own eye; but as this only showed what man, when unrestrained, is in his present condition, they were quite pertinent to the apostle's purpose. <div eID="gen31793" type="x-p"/>
entries.e00ac40af24676477c676865bf3f621841054628: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16393"/><div sID="gen31794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16393"/><hi type="bold">13-18. Their, &c.--</hi>From generals, the apostle here comes to particulars, culling from different parts of Scripture passages which speak of depravity as it affects the different members of the body; as if to show more affectingly how "from the sole of the foot even to the head there is no soundness" in us.<div eID="gen31794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">throat is an open sepulchre--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Psa 5:9</reference>); that is, "What proceeds out of their heart, and finds vent in speech and action through the throat, is like the pestilential breath of an open grave."<div eID="gen31795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with their tongues they have used deceit--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Psa 5:9</reference>); that is, "That tongue which is man's glory (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.9">Psa 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.57.8">57:8</reference>) is prostituted to the purposes of deception."<div eID="gen31796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the poison of asps is under their lips--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.140.3">Psa 140:3</reference>): that is, "Those lips which should 'drop as an honeycomb,' and 'feed many,' and 'give thanks unto His name' (<reference osisRef="Song.4.11">So 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.10.21">Pr 10:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">He 13:15</reference>), are employed to secrete and to dart deadly poison." <div eID="gen31797" type="x-p"/>
entries.851ce9ce2d5faa5a6ad2aa991b3524be2a1e3f0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16398"/><div sID="gen31802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16398"/><hi type="bold">19. Now we know that what ... the law--</hi>that is, the Scriptures, considered as a law of duty.<div eID="gen31802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saith, it saith to them that are under the law--</hi>of course, therefore, to the Jews.<div eID="gen31803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that every mouth--</hi>opened in self-justification.<div eID="gen31804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">may be stopped, and all the world may become--</hi>that is, be seen to be, and own itself.<div eID="gen31805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31806" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">guilty--</hi>and so condemned<div eID="gen31806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31807" type="x-p"/> before God. <div eID="gen31807" type="x-p"/>
entries.faf52acc2b150247c6d977f76bea986b10dfe978: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16399"/><div sID="gen31808" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16399"/><hi type="bold">20. Therefore by the deeds of--</hi>obedience to<div eID="gen31808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the law there shall no flesh be justified--</hi>that is, be held and treated as righteous; as is plain from the whole scope and strain of the argument.<div eID="gen31809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in his sight--</hi>at His bar (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.2">Psa 143:2</reference>).<div eID="gen31810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for by the law is the knowledge of sin--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Rom.4.15">Ro 4:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.7.7">Ro 7:7</reference>; and <reference osisRef="1John.3.4">1Jo 3:4</reference>).<div eID="gen31811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Note, How broad and deep does the apostle in this section lay the foundations of his great doctrine of Justification by free grace--</hi>in the disorder of man's whole nature, the consequent universality of human guilt, the condemnation, by reason of the breach of divine law, of the whole world, and the impossibility of justification before God by obedience to that violated law! Only when these humiliating conclusions are accepted and felt, are we in a condition to appreciate and embrace the grace of the Gospel, next to be opened up. <div eID="gen31812" type="x-p"/>
entries.efdf1fbd3632edd34fb26466963f586e8870a932: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16400"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Rom.3.21-Rom.3.26">Ro 3:21-26</reference>. God's Justifying Righteousness through Faith in Jesus Christ, Alike Adapted to Our Necessities and Worthy of Himself.</title> <div sID="gen31813" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16400"/><hi type="bold">21-23. But now the righteousness of God--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Ro 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen31813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without the law--</hi>that is, a righteousness to which our obedience to the law contributes nothing whatever (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.28">Ro 3:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.16">Ga 2:16</reference>).<div eID="gen31814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is manifested, being witnessed--</hi>attested.<div eID="gen31815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the law and the prophets--</hi>the Old Testament Scriptures. Thus this justifying righteousness, though new, as only now fully disclosed, is an old righteousness, predicted and foreshadowed in the Old Testament. <div eID="gen31816" type="x-p"/>
entries.acc5d8716c1af01e98f9af96d307c912981584bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16403"/><div sID="gen31823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16403"/><hi type="bold">24. justified freely--</hi>without anything done on our part to deserve.<div eID="gen31823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31824" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by his grace--</hi>His free love.<div eID="gen31824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus--</hi>a most important clause; teaching us that though justification is quite gratuitous, it is not a mere fiat of the divine will, but based on a "Redemption," that is, "the payment of a Ransom," in Christ's death. That this is the sense of the word "redemption," when applied to Christ's death, will appear clear to any impartial student of the passages where it occurs. <div eID="gen31825" type="x-p"/>
entries.28edcca72fc702e575dd9307b307581663c5cf10: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16404"/><div sID="gen31826" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16404"/><hi type="bold">25-26. Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation--</hi>or "propitiatory sacrifice."<div eID="gen31826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31827" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through faith in his blood--</hi>Some of the best interpreters, observing that "faith upon" is the usual phrase in Greek, not "faith in" Christ, would place a "comma" after "faith," and understand the words as if written thus: "to be a propitiation, in His blood, through faith." But "faith in Christ" is used in <reference osisRef="Gal.3.26">Ga 3:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="Eph.1.15">Ep 1:15</reference>; and "faith in His blood" is the natural and appropriate meaning here.<div eID="gen31827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to declare his righteousness for the remission--</hi>rather, "pretermission" or "passing by."<div eID="gen31828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31829" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of sins--</hi>"the sins."<div eID="gen31829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31830" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that are past--</hi>not the sins committed by the believer before he embraces Christ, but the sins committed under the old economy, before Christ came to "put away sin by the sacrifice of Himself."<div eID="gen31830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through the forbearance of God--</hi>God not remitting but only forbearing to punish them, or passing them by, until an adequate atonement for them should be made. In thus not imputing them, God was righteous, but He was not seen to be so; there was no "manifestation of His righteousness" in doing so under the ancient economy. But now that God can "set forth" Christ as a "propitiation for sin through faith in His blood," the righteousness of His procedure in passing by the sins of believers before, and in now remitting them, is "manifested," declared, brought fully out to the view of the whole world. (Our translators have unfortunately missed this glorious truth, taking "the sins that are past" to mean the past sins of believers--committed before faith--and rendering, by the word "remission," what means only a "passing by"; thus making it appear that "remission of sins" is "through the forbearance of God," which it certainly is not). <div eID="gen31831" type="x-p"/>
entries.36571c81673f319955df595965e7beccd1960524: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16406"/><div sID="gen31836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16406"/><hi type="bold">27-28. Where is boasting then? ... excluded. By what law?--</hi>on what principle or scheme?.<div eID="gen31836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31837" type="x-p"/> of works? Nay; but by the law of faith. <div eID="gen31837" type="x-p"/>
entries.cef58424af11a7e7037db55d4784e076762097c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16408"/><div sID="gen31843" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16408"/><hi type="bold">29. Is he the God of the Jews only? &c.--</hi>The way of salvation must be one equally suited to the whole family of fallen man: but the doctrine of justification by faith is the only one that lays the basis of a Universal Religion; this therefore is another mark of its truth. <div eID="gen31843" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d1909aba459e0359dd7d523a5a380fb17db90f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16409"/><div sID="gen31844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16409"/><hi type="bold">30. it is one God who shall justify--</hi>"has unchangeably fixed that He shall justify."<div eID="gen31844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the circumcision by--</hi>"of"<div eID="gen31845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faith, and the uncircumcision through faith--</hi>probably this is but a varied statement of the same truth for greater emphasis (see <reference osisRef="Rom.3.22">Ro 3:22</reference>); though Bengel thinks that the justification of the Jews, as the born heirs of the promise, may be here purposely said to be "of faith," while that of the Gentiles, previously "strangers to the covenants of promise," may be said to be "through faith," as thus admitted into a new family.<div eID="gen31846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31847" type="x-p"/> Objection: <div eID="gen31847" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f363ecf9b200e9a4af60b6278c589cf24be176b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16410"/><div sID="gen31848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16410"/><hi type="bold">31. Do we then make void the law through faith?--</hi>"Does this doctrine of justification by faith, then, dissolve the obligation of the law? If so, it cannot be of God. But away with such a thought, for it does just the reverse."<div eID="gen31848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31849" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God forbid: yea, we establish the law--</hi>It will be observed here, that, important as was this objection, and opening up as it did so noble a field for the illustration of the peculiar glory of the Gospel, the apostle does no more here than indignantly repel it, intending at a subsequent stage of his argument (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.1-Rom.6.23">Ro 6:1-23</reference>) to resume and discuss it at length.<div eID="gen31849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Note, (1) It is a fundamental requisite of all true religion that it tend to humble the sinner and exalt God; and every system which breeds self-righteousness, or cherishes boasting, bears falsehood on its face (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.27">Ro 3:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.28">28</reference>). (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">2</reference>) The fitness of the Gospel to be a universal religion, beneath which the guilty of every name and degree are invited and warranted to take shelter and repose, is a glorious evidence of its truth (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.29">Ro 3:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.30">30</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.3">3</reference>) The glory of God's law, in its eternal and immutable obligations, is then only fully apprehended by the sinner, and then only is it enthroned in the depths of his soul, when, believing that "He was made sin for him who knew no sin," he sees himself "made the righteousness of God in Him" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>). Thus do we not make void the law through faith: yea, we establish the law. (4) This chapter, and particularly the latter part of it, "is the proper seat of the Pauline doctrine of Justification, and the grand proof-passage of the Protestant doctrine of the Imputation of Christ's righteousness and of Justification not on account of, but through faith alone" [Philippi]. To make good this doctrine, and reseat it in the faith and affection of the Church, was worth all the bloody struggles that it cost our fathers, and it will be the wisdom and safety, the life and vigor of the churches, to "stand fast in this liberty wherewith Christ hath made them free, and not be again entangled"--</hi>in the very least degree--"with the yoke of bondage" (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.1">Ga 5:1</reference>). <chapter eID="Rom.3"/>

entries.e96e3908aaea4d66d960d62ed07509bd6aea69ff: <div eID="gen46072" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen46073" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen46074" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen46074" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen46073" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen46075" type="x-p"/> The apostle points out the peculiar privileges of the Jews, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.1-Rom.3.8">Rom 3:1-8</reference>. But shows that they, also, as well as the Gentiles, had sinned, and forfeited all right and title to God's especial favor, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.9">Rom 3:9</reference>. The corrupt state of all mankind, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.10-Rom.3.18">Rom 3:10-18</reference>. All the world is guilty before God, and none can be justified by the works of the law, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.19">Rom 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.20">Rom 3:20</reference>. God's Mercy in providing redemption for a lost world, by Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.21-Rom.3.26">Rom 3:21-26</reference>. This excludes boasting on the part both of Jew and Gentile; provides salvation through faith for both; and does not set aside, but establishes the law, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.27-Rom.3.31">Rom 3:27-31</reference>. <div eID="gen46075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46076" type="x-p"/> Dr. Taylor observes: - "In the preceding chapter the apostle has carried his argument to the utmost length: what remains is to keep the Jew in temper, to fix his convictions, and to draw the grand conclusion. "He has shown that the Jews were more wicked than the Gentiles; that their possession of the law, circumcision, and outward profession of relation to God, were no ground of acceptance with him. This was in effect to say that the Jews had forfeited their right to the privileges of God's peculiar people, and that they were as unworthy to be continued in the Church as the Gentiles were to be taken into it; and consequently, in order to their enjoying the privileges of the Church under the Messiah, they stood in need of a fresh display of grace, which if they rejected, God would cast them out of the vineyard. The apostle was sensible that the Jew would understand what he said in this sense; and that it must be very irritating to him to hear that his law, circumcision, and all his external advantages, were utterly insufficient to procure him the favor of God. This at once stripped him of all his peculiar honors and privileges; and the apostle, who had often argued with his countrymen on these points, knew what they would be ready to say on this subject; and, therefore, introduces a dialogue between himself and a Jew, in which he gives him leave to answer and defend himself. In this dialogue the apostle undoubtedly refers to the rejection of the Jews, which he considers at large in the ninth, tenth, and eleventh chapters. After the dialogue is finished, he resumes his argument, and proves, by their own Scriptures, that the Jews were guilty as well as other men; and that no part of mankind could have any right to the blessings of God's kingdom by any works which they had performed, but merely through the propitiatory sacrifice offered by Christ; and that this, far from destroying the law, was just the thing that the law required, and by which its claims were established. "The sum and force of the apostle's argument is this: All sorts of men, Jews as well as Gentiles, have sinned; therefore, none of them can lay claim to the blessings of his kingdom on the ground of obedience. The Jew, therefore, stands as much in need of God's grace to give him a title to those blessings as the Gentile; and, consequently, the Gentile has as good a title as the Jew. And, when all are in the same circumstances, it is perfectly absurd for any to pretend to engross it to themselves, exclusively of others, who are only as bad as they. "Thus the apostle solidly proves that we, Gentiles, through faith alone, have a good and firm title to all the blessings of the Gospel covenant - election, adoption, pardon, privileges, ordinances, the Holy Spirit, and the hope of eternal life." <div eID="gen46076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46077" type="x-p"/> As the nine first verses are a dialogue between the apostle and a Jew, I shall prefix the speakers to their respective questions and answers, to make the whole the more intelligible to the reader. <div eID="gen46077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46078" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen46078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46079" type="x-p"/> Jew. What advantage then hath the Jew? Or what profit is there of circumcision? - As if he had said: You lately allowed, (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.25">Rom 2:25</reference>), that circumcision verily profited; but if circumcision, or our being in covenant with God, raises us no higher in the Divine favor than the Gentiles; if the virtuous among them are as acceptable as any of us; nay, and condemn our nation too, as no longer deserving the Divine regards; pray tell me, wherein lies the superior honor of the Jew; and what benefit can arise to him from his circumcision, and being vested in the privileges of God's peculiar people?
entries.30b9a87dad2548d516adf514a9effa9a457727bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen46079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46080" type="x-p"/> Apostle. Much every way - The Jews, in reference to the means and motives of obedience, enjoy many advantages beyond the Gentiles; and, principally, because to them were committed the oracles of God - that revelation of his will to Moses and the prophets, containing a treasure of excellencies, with which no other part of the world has been favored; though they have most grievously abused these privileges.
entries.8427c2827180e356670b8e3b2e5e2b0db72f6a1b: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen46080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46081" type="x-p"/> Jew. For what - τι γαρ, What then, if some did not believe, etc. If some of the Jewish nation have abused their privileges, and acted contrary to their obligations, shall their wickedness annul the Promise which God made to Abraham, that he would, by an everlasting covenant, be a God to him and to his seed after him? <reference osisRef="Gen.17.7">Gen 17:7</reference>. Shall God, therefore, by stripping the Jews of their peculiar honor, as you intimate he will, falsify his promise to the nation, because some of the Jews are bad men?
entries.b512817aa88f576fe424b919ab8430e01e1f37db: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen46081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46082" type="x-p"/> Apostle. God forbid - μη γενοιτο, Let it not be, far from it, by no means.
